btc.name: Bitcoin
btc.reason: Public, value-only, settlement-grade: the most credible neutral money network.

ln.name: Bitcoin Lightning
ln.tagline: BTC at retail speed · sub-cent fees
ln.reason: You want public BTC payments but with consumer-grade throughput — Lightning is Bitcoin's L2 for that.

eth.name: Ethereum L1
eth.reason: Public, contract-driven, settlement-grade — Ethereum L1 is the canonical choice for high-value composable DeFi.

arb.name: Ethereum L2 (Arbitrum / Base)
arb.reason: Same EVM, much lower fees, inherits Ethereum security via fraud proofs. The default for medium-throughput dApps.

sol.name: Solana
sol.reason: High throughput + low fees + native ecosystem of consumer-grade dApps. Trade-off: fewer, more powerful validators.

avax.name: Avalanche L1
avax.reason: Sub-second finality with the option to launch a sovereign L1 (subnet) while plugging into the Primary Network.

cosmos.name: Cosmos zone
cosmos.reason: You want full control over consensus + gas + governance, and you're happy to bootstrap your own validators. Cosmos SDK + IBC.

fabric.name: Hyperledger Fabric
fabric.reason: Permissioned membership + channels for selective data sharing — purpose-built for known-party B2B consortia.

stark.name: Starknet (ZK)
stark.reason: Cairo VM with STARK validity proofs and tooling for ZK credential proofs. Note: Starknet itself is public; its proofs give cheap verification, not hidden transactions. For hidden state, see Aztec.

aztec.name: Aztec Network
aztec.reason: Native encrypted state on Ethereum — every tx hides amount + sender by default. The strongest privacy primitive on EVM-adjacent infra.

xrpl.name: XRP Ledger
xrpl.reason: Payment-optimised L1 with a native DEX and Trust Lines. Suited to cross-border settlement, tokenised assets and FX rails.

zkp.heading: Zero-Knowledge Proofs — the one idea
zkp.subtitle: One sentence and one everyday example.
zkp.oneLinerB: without revealing anything that makes it true.
zkp.exampleSubtitle: Same goal, two ways. Watch what the bouncer learns.
zkp.withoutBodyStrong: name, address, nationality and exact birth date
zkp.withoutCaption: You proved one fact and leaked five.

demo.pick: Pick how you prove you're over 18:
demo.idle: Choose an option on the left…

more.text: Log in by proving you know the password — without typing it anywhere.
Prove your salary clears a mortgage threshold — without handing over the payslip.
Prove you are one unique human — without saying which human.

zkpCave.heading: Where's Waldo? — the same idea, visually
zkpCave.subtitle: I prove I found Waldo on a crowded page without telling you where he is.

steps.title: The claim
steps.text: I say I found Waldo on this crowded page. You don't believe me, and I refuse to point, because that gives my answer away.

steps.title: The proof
steps.text: I cover the whole page with a large opaque sheet that has one tiny Waldo-sized hole, lined up exactly over him. You see Waldo through the hole.

steps.title: You're convinced
steps.text: Waldo is clearly on the page. But the sheet hid the rest, so you still have no idea where on the page he is.

zkpCave.punchlineA: you end fully convinced Waldo is there, yet learn
zkpCave.punchlineB: about his location. That gap is "zero-knowledge".
zkpCave.classicBody: "the magic cave": Alice repeatedly exits the side a verifier shouts, proving she knows the password without ever saying it. Repeat enough and luck is ruled out.

zkApps.heading: ZK in production today
zkApps.subtitle: Each card is a live product or protocol.

props.d: If you really are over 18, the proof always works.
No clever trick lets a 16-year-old forge the proof.
The checker learns the yes/no — and nothing more.

items.name: ZK rollups
items.does: Let Ethereum check thousands of transactions by verifying one small proof — fees in cents, withdrawals in hours instead of a week.

items.name: Proof of personhood
items.does: Prove to an app that you are a unique human — without revealing which human.

items.name: Private payments
items.does: Send money where sender, receiver and amount stay hidden, yet the network still proves the payment is valid.

items.name: Proof of reserves
items.does: Let an exchange prove it holds every customer's deposit — without publishing any customer's balance.

items.name: zkEmail
items.does: Prove an email says something — a payment confirmation, a ticket, a password reset — without showing the email or your inbox.

items.name: zkTLS / web proofs
items.does: Prove a fact from any website you log into (bank balance above X, your driver rating) without sharing your password or a screenshot.

items.name: zkLogin
items.does: Sign in to a blockchain app with your Google or Apple account — without that identity being linked to you on-chain.

items.name: Private voting
items.does: Vote in an election anyone can audit, where nobody — not even the organiser — can see your ballot.

items.name: Compliance proofs
items.does: Prove your funds do not come from a flagged source — without revealing your transaction history. Returns in the privacy chapter.

zkApps.families: SNARKs (tiny proofs, one-off setup ceremony — Zcash, zkSync) and STARKs (bigger proofs, no setup, quantum-resistant — Starknet). For a business decision the difference rarely matters; for an engineer it does.

zkIdentity.heading: KYC without handing over your identity
zkIdentity.subtitle: Step by step. Any ZK-capable platform can run this pattern.

flow.holds: verifies you once · signs a credential
keeps the credential · makes the proof

business: No database of passports to leak — far less GDPR exposure
Onboarding in seconds, reusable across every service that trusts the issuer
Regulators still get what they need: proof the check was done, on demand

kycSteps.label: Bank issues a credential
kycSteps.desc: Your bank verifies you once and signs a digital credential: name, date of birth, residency, sanctions check. It lives in your wallet — only you hold it.

kycSteps.label: You generate a proof
kycSteps.desc: Your wallet builds a proof: "signed by the bank · age ≥ 18 · EU resident · not sanctioned." The proof contains none of the raw data.

kycSteps.label: The app verifies
kycSteps.desc: The app's smart contract checks the proof and lets you in. Your name and birth date never leave your wallet — not even the app operator can read them.

starknetCompare.kycFootStrong: private voting · proof of solvency · medical records · sanctions screening
starknetCompare.kycFootB: — anywhere the question is "is this true?" without "who are you?".

l2Why.heading: The trilemma — and why Layer 2s appeared
l2Why.subtitle: A chain can be open, hard to attack and cheap, but not all three at once. Layer 2 keeps the first two on L1 and adds the third on top.

corners.name: Open to everyone
corners.biz: no single owner · anyone can verify

triangle.l2Label: L2 adds this corner on top

l2Why.analogy: You don't take every coffee purchase to court; you use a card terminal and go to court only for disputes. L1 is the court (slow, final, trusted); L2 is the terminal that reports back to it.
l2Why.problemB: . When demand spikes, a simple swap can cost
l2Why.problemC: . Consumer apps, games and micro-payments cannot run there.
l2Why.ideaC: back to L1. Ethereum stays the judge; the work happens where it's cheap.

steps.title: Execute off-chain
steps.text: Thousands of users transact on the L2 — fast and near-free. The L2 sequencer orders and runs them.

steps.title: Batch & prove
steps.text: The L2 compresses the batch and produces a proof of what happened (a fraud proof window, or a validity proof).

steps.title: Settle on L1
steps.text: The batch + proof is posted to Ethereum. L1 enforces correctness, so the L2 inherits L1-grade security.

shared: Execute transactions off-chain, post compressed data to Ethereum L1
Inherit Ethereum's security — L1 is the final arbiter
10–100× cheaper than L1 for end users
Native bridges back to L1 (with different withdrawal times)
ERC-20 tokens and ETH work on both

choose.rest: Use Arbitrum or Optimism — fastest path to deploy existing Solidity.
Use a ZK rollup — users don't want to wait 7 days to withdraw.
Neither rollup type is private by default. ZK proofs are the ingredient, but you need a privacy-first design (Aztec, Zcash-style) on top.

dataAvail.heading: Why rollups post their data to Ethereum
dataAvail.subtitle: A proof shows the batch was correct. The data is what lets you leave if the rollup's operator disappears.

svg.l1Sub: stores both · anyone can read them
svg.userSub: rebuild your balance from L1 data and withdraw, operator or not
svg.caption: Proof without data: you know the books balance but cannot see your own line. The data is what makes the exit possible.

cards.title: What gets posted
cards.desc: Not just a result. A compressed copy of every L2 transaction goes to Ethereum; since 2024 it travels in cheap 'blobs' that Ethereum keeps for about 18 days, long enough for anyone to copy.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.desc: If the rollup's servers go dark, anyone can read the data from Ethereum, rebuild every balance and prove theirs to the L1 bridge to withdraw. Without the data your coins are stuck even though the proof was valid.

cards.title: The cheaper shortcut
cards.desc: Some chains post data to a separate network (Celestia) or a small committee instead. Fees fall, but you now also trust that group to keep the data. Such chains are called validiums or optimiums, and L2BEAT lists them apart from rollups.

privacy.subtitle: Every address, balance and transfer is visible to anyone, forever. Pseudonymous is not anonymous: one link to your name unlocks your whole history.

privacyApproaches.heading: Four ways to get privacy on-chain
privacyApproaches.subtitle: Each makes a different trade-off between strength, flexibility, and how regulators treat it.

items.name: Zcash
items.mech: Optional shielded transactions use zk-SNARKs to prove ownership and value conservation without revealing sender, recipient or amount.
items.trade: Privacy is opt-in, so most volume stays transparent — weakening the anonymity set.

items.name: Monero
items.mech: Mandatory privacy: ring signatures hide the sender, stealth addresses hide the recipient, RingCT hides the amount.
items.trade: No transparency option — auditing is hard, so many exchanges have delisted it.

items.name: Aztec · Aleo
items.mech: Smart contracts with private state and inputs — build any confidential dApp, not just private payments.
items.trade: Far more flexible, but newer tooling (Noir, Leo) and privacy lives at the contract level.

items.name: Mixers
items.mech: Pool many deposits, withdraw to fresh addresses — breaking the on-chain link between sender and receiver.
items.trade: Credibly neutral and immutable — which is exactly why they became a sanctions target.

privacyRegulation.heading: Tornado Cash — when privacy code met the law
privacyRegulation.subtitle: One mixer, one sanction, and years of courts deciding where a privacy tool ends and laundering infrastructure begins.

story.d: A non-custodial mixer on Ethereum: deposit, wait, withdraw to a fresh address. Nobody operates it — the code simply runs.
The US Treasury sanctioned the smart-contract addresses themselves — a first. Its reason: ~$7B laundered, including $455M by North Korea's Lazarus Group. Ordinary users were swept in too.
Alexey Pertsev convicted in the Netherlands (64 months, under appeal); Roman Storm awaiting trial in the US. Writing privacy software itself became the legal question.
A US appeals court ruled immutable smart contracts are not "property" that can be sanctioned. OFAC delisted Tornado Cash on 21 March 2025.
Storm convicted on one count (unlicensed money transmission); the jury hung on laundering and sanctions charges. Samourai Wallet's founders received 4–5 years (Nov 2025).

privacyRegulation.truthsLabel: Two things are true at once
privacyRegulation.truthA: Privacy tools really did shield a state-sponsored hacking group's loot. Regulators had a genuine problem.
privacyRegulation.truthB: The same tools protected ordinary people from surveillance — and sanctioning code punished users who had done nothing wrong.
privacyRegulation.cypherpunkLabel: Back to where this course began
privacyRegulation.cypherpunk: The Cypherpunks (Course 01) said privacy is a precondition for freedom; regulators say untraceable money is a precondition for crime. Both are partly right, which is why selective disclosure (next slide) matters.
privacyRegulation.recapFreedom: Course 01 · Prologue — the Cypherpunks: privacy as a precondition for freedom
privacyRegulation.guidanceC: (e.g. prove "not on a sanctions list" without revealing identity) over all-or-nothing anonymity.

quiz.question: A user withdraws funds from Arbitrum (an optimistic rollup) back to Ethereum L1. The standard withdrawal takes ~7 days. Why?
options: L1 block time is slower than L2 block time, so L1 must catch up before processing the withdrawal.

Optimistic rollups assume transactions valid by default. The 7-day "challenge window" lets anyone submit a fraud proof if the L2 state is invalid; until that window closes, withdrawals can't be safely finalised on L1.
Arbitrum batches withdrawals weekly to amortise gas costs across users.
Ethereum L1 deliberately rate-limits L2 withdrawals to prevent rollup-induced congestion.
quiz.explanation: The delay is structural. The sequencer posts state roots to L1 assumed valid; anyone watching can challenge an invalid root with a fraud proof during the window. Until it closes, L1 cannot trust the root enough to release withdrawals. ZK rollups ship a validity proof with each batch, so withdrawals finalise in one L1 block. Third-party fast bridges (Across, Hop, Stargate) let users skip the wait for a small premium.

quiz2.question: A team is launching a new app-specific blockchain. They need full control over consensus algorithm, gas token, and upgrade governance. Which model best fits — and what's the trade-off?
options: Polkadot parachain via Coretime — sovereignty within the relay chain's shared security envelope, no trade-off.
Cosmos zone via Cosmos SDK — full sovereignty over consensus, gas, and upgrades; the trade-off is bootstrapping their own validator set without inheriting any external security.
Avalanche L1 — sovereign chains, but they must use Snowman consensus and pay AVAX-denominated subscription fees.
All three give equal sovereignty; the decision is purely cost-driven.
quiz2.explanation: Cosmos zones are sovereign by design: each picks its consensus engine, gas token, governance and upgrade rules. The trade-off is real: the team must recruit validators and bootstrap a token to pay them. Polkadot parachains share the Relay Chain's validators but must conform to its runtime model and Coretime schedule. Avalanche L1s (formerly Subnets) allow custom VMs and validator sets, but most run Snowman variants and pay validator fees in AVAX. Shared security versus sovereignty is a trade-off, not a tier list.

takeaways.title: Section 05 — Key Takeaways
items: Zero-knowledge in one line: prove something is true without revealing what makes it true — and it is already live (ZK rollups, World ID, Zcash, proof of reserves, zkLogin, private voting)
The trilemma explains Layer 2: L1 stays the slow, trusted court; L2s are the fast, cheap lane that reports back to it
Optimistic rollups (Arbitrum, Base) = full EVM + 7-day exit; ZK rollups (zkSync, Starknet, Scroll) = maths-checked exits in hours — neither is private by default
Public chains are transparent by default; privacy needs extra cryptography — and the Tornado Cash story shows the law is still catching up
Run five questions before picking a platform: permission, programmability, throughput, privacy, and sovereignty

keyPoints.s5-zkp: Prove it is true without showing why.
keyPoints.s5-zkp-cave: A proof convinces by making cheating impossible, not by showing the secret.
keyPoints.s5-zk-apps: ZK is a product, not a paper: scaling, identity, solvency and compliance proofs are live today.
keyPoints.s5-zk-identity: Verify the claim, not the person: the issuer vouches once and the customer reveals only what each service needs.
keyPoints.s5-l2-why: You cannot max out speed, cost and decentralisation at once; L2s buy speed by borrowing L1 security.
keyPoints.s5-layer2: Optimistic rollups are innocent until proven guilty (7-day exit), ZK rollups are proven before accepted (hours), and neither is private by default.
keyPoints.s5-data-avail: A rollup is only as safe as the data behind it; posting every transaction to Ethereum is what lets users leave without the operator's help.
keyPoints.s5-starknet: Starknet uses ZK for cheap verification, not secrecy.
keyPoints.s5-polkadot: Polkadot rents out security; parachains skip recruiting validators but live by the Relay Chain's rules.
keyPoints.s5-avalanche: Avalanche sells sovereign lanes with shared tooling; a custom L1 is only as secure as its own validators.
keyPoints.s5-privacy: A public ledger is a permanent record; privacy has to be added on purpose.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-approaches: Mixers hide everything or nothing; ZK reveals exactly what a counterparty needs.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-regulation: Untraceable money shields dissidents and launderers alike; selective disclosure is the way out.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-future: Keep the data confidential and still prove you follow the rules.
keyPoints.s5-evaluate: Judge a project by who built it, what the code says and who holds the tokens.
keyPoints.s5-evaluate-2: Locked liquidity, honest docs and organic on-chain usage; ten minutes with free tools beats any influencer thread.
keyPoints.s5-decision: Five questions beat a hundred logos: permission, programmability, throughput, privacy, sovereignty.

starknet.heading: Starknet — a ZK rollup on Ethereum
starknet.subtitle: Thousands of transactions run off-chain; one STARK proof tells Ethereum they were all executed correctly.
starknet.recap: Section 02 · Rollups & L2s — and the ZK chapter above

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: Ethereum's security, Starknet's speed
cards.body: A Layer 2 that batches transactions, proves the batch with a STARK and posts only the proof to Ethereum. If the proof is wrong, Ethereum rejects the batch — no waiting period, no trust in the operator.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Cheap verification + smart wallets
cards.body: Fees 10–100× below L1 and withdrawals in hours, not a week. Every account is a smart contract by default (account abstraction): social recovery, session keys, fees paid in any token.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: Ekubo — a DEX from a former Uniswap lead
cards.body: A concentrated-liquidity exchange with the deepest liquidity on Starknet. Fully on-chain games (Realms: Eternum, Loot Survivor) are the other main use.

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Public by default, Cairo only
cards.body: ZK here buys cheap verification, not secrecy — transactions are as visible as on Ethereum. Apps must be written in Cairo, so Solidity code cannot be copied over unchanged, and the ecosystem is far smaller than Arbitrum or Base.

polkadot.heading: Polkadot — security for rent
polkadot.subtitle: A Layer 0: one Relay Chain whose validators secure every connected parachain at once.

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: One validator set, many chains
cards.body: Parachains are purpose-built L1s that rent block time (Coretime) on the Relay Chain instead of recruiting their own validators. The Relay Chain's ~300 validators finalise all of them together.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Day-one security and native cross-chain calls
cards.body: A new chain is as secure as Polkadot the moment it connects. Parachains talk to each other through XCM — a built-in message format — so no bridge contract and no wrapped token inside the ecosystem.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: Moonbeam — Ethereum apps, Polkadot plumbing
cards.body: An EVM-compatible parachain where Solidity contracts deploy unchanged and can call other parachains over XCM. It is the usual entry point for Ethereum teams testing the ecosystem.

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Rules of the club, and a thin crowd
cards.body: Chains must follow Relay Chain rules and pay for coretime in DOT; user and developer traction has lagged Ethereum's L2s; and reaching chains outside Polkadot still needs a bridge (Snowbridge to Ethereum).

avalanche.heading: Avalanche — sovereign lanes, shared tooling
avalanche.subtitle: A Layer 0 whose Primary Network coordinates custom 'Avalanche L1s', each with its own validators and rules.

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: A primary network plus custom L1s
cards.body: Three built-in chains (X, P and the EVM C-Chain, where DeFi lives) plus any number of Avalanche L1s (formerly Subnets): sovereign chains that pick their own validators, gas token and rules, coordinated by the P-Chain.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Sub-second finality and your own lane
cards.body: Snowman consensus settles in under a second. A game or a bank can launch its own L1 with custom fees and permissioning, reuse Ethereum tooling, and message other L1s natively through Avalanche Warp.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: JP Morgan on a permissioned L1
cards.body: JP Morgan's Onyx (now Kinexys) and Apollo tested tokenised-portfolio management on Avalanche's institutional 'Evergreen Spruce' network under Singapore's Project Guardian (2023).

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Small validator sets, fragmented liquidity
cards.body: A sovereign L1 is only as secure as its own validators, often a handful. Finality is probabilistic (a tiny chance of reversal, unlike BFT's hard guarantee), and most liquidity still sits on the C-Chain.
